source.title: Quantifying the Gain in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
source.authors: Moses Charikar; Chirag Pabbaraju; Kirankumar Shiragur

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plotted results have no extractable numerical values in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives new theoretical results and regression experiments on weak-to-strong training. It tests the same general question using squared-error gain and misfit rather than Burns et al.'s PGR measure, and refines the claim to particular assumptions and task settings.
record.gate_note: The experiments report gain-versus-misfit plots, mostly without numerical point values. The paper's discussion of auxiliary losses and classification results cites Burns et al.; those are not this study's results. The heuristic-selection tables report errors for weakly supervised models, but do not provide a direct weak-supervisor comparison or PGR.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own weak-to-strong pipelines: weak models trained on true labels, then strong linear heads trained on weak labels. It measures gain over the weak supervisor on synthetic, molecular and NLP regression tasks. It also proves conditions (Theorems 1–2) under which the student must beat the supervisor. This bears on V1, V3 and V5 with a different measure (squared-error gain vs misfit) rather than PGR.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. More precisely, the authors conclude that in regression with squared loss and a convex finetuning class, a weakly supervised strong model provably improves on its weak supervisor by at least its misfit on the weak labels; empirically the gain is roughly equal to the misfit. Experiments suggest this holds beyond convex classes, and weak/strong roles should be set by representation quality, not expressive power. They also propose misfit-based selection among weak supervisors and do not address classification.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the weak-label fine-tuning pipeline, but studies regression with squared loss and representation/task-function setups rather than Burns et al.'s original task suite and PGR measure. The paper's own empirical metric is gain in accuracy/error reduction plotted against misfit.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with representation quality and data available for representation learning; the nominal roles reverse when a simpler model learns the better representation. Experiments also vary weak-model architecture and dataset/task.
record.problems: Most empirical results are conveyed in plots without point values or stated uncertainty. The main experiments use regression and squared loss; PGR and a strong model trained on true labels as a ceiling are not reported. The paper identifies convexity as necessary for its theorems, and its real-world experiments are not large-scale modern-model evaluations.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional weak-model-selection error tables for Lipop (Table 1) and ESOL/FreeSolv (Appendix B, Tables 2–3). These are omitted because they assess the proposed selection heuristic and do not provide a direct weak-supervisor comparison or PGR. Figure 5 contains separate weak-model configuration series for each of six essay rubrics; the rows retain rubric-level plotted outcomes rather than transcribing every plotted configuration because exact point values are not stated.

untested.parts: PGR and a strong model trained on true labels as ceiling; classification tasks; large modern LLMs.
No auxiliary loss, ensembling or loss-variant experiments; auxiliary losses are only discussed via Burns et al.
Chess and reward modelling; systematic scaling of student size; classification tasks.
Exploitation of supervisor blind spots, distribution shift, and correlated errors (only discussed, Appendix E).
Classification, non-squared losses, and non-convex task classes (theory does not cover them).

missing.what: Weak-supervisor selection tables. For each weak hidden size they give weak error − misfit vs the strong student's true error. Misfit-based ranking picks the best student on Lipop and ESOL but not exactly on FreeSolv, and some bounds are negative (e.g. ESOL dim 96: −0.888 vs true error 1.391), showing the theory's error terms are non-negligible. rows_left_out dismisses these, but they bear on what predicts the student's outcome (V3) and on the theorem's bound in practice (V5).

record.verdict_notes: Gain (weak error − student error) is the PGR numerator, so its sign suffices for V1 even without a ceiling. Rows r14/r15 are designed strong-to-weak swaps and are removed from V1. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not calculate PGR or compare against a strong model trained on true labels as a ceiling. Its experiments concern real-valued regression and squared loss, not classification.
No auxiliary-confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembling, or loss-variant experiment is conducted.
The study varies representation architectures, sizes and data availability in regression experiments, but does not test chess or reward modelling.
No distribution-shift test or test of exploiting what a weak supervisor cannot check is reported; correlated-error effects are discussed by reference to Burns et al., not tested here.

The theory concerns real-valued regression with squared loss and a convex task-function class (with a finite-sample, non-realizable extension). It does not establish conditions for other losses or classification.

statements.correction: Positive-gain settings: Figures 2, 5, 6 and 7. Figure 3: reversed representation quality and negative gain. Figure 7: non-convex heads using sigmoid, tanh or ReLU.
statements.problem: All plotted settings is too broad: Figure 3 contains negative-gain role-reversal settings. The cited r17 also uses a sigmoid after the linear map, rather than a purely linear head.

statements.correction: T=5; Nr=250; Nf=2000. The 2-layer model learns a better representation than the 8-layer model. Figure 3c supports representation-quality dependence under V3.
statements.problem: The architecture sizes, sample conditions and negative gain are correct, but the authors identify reversed weak/strong roles; this is not a failure with an actually stronger student.

statements.correction: Section 5.3: T=5 and Nr=250 produce better representations in the simpler model; Figure 3c resembles the explicit role swaps. V3: supports.
statements.problem: The low-sample finding is accurately described, but it supports V3's dependence on representations rather than limiting a claim that larger models must always be stronger.

statements.correction: Appendix B: weak error minus misfit is sometimes negative despite positive student error. The authors infer non-negligible Theorem 2 error terms. No failure of the full corrected bound is established.
statements.problem: For this study, the real-data discrepancy concerns the comparison after omitting error terms; it is not evidence that the full conditional theorem fails.

statements.correction: Positive-gain settings: Figures 2, 5, 6 and 7. Figure 7 uses nonlinear activations after linear maps. Figure 3c: the 2-layer supervisor has the better representation. reader_labels.reason: The paper finds that a less expressive model can have the better representation in scarce-data settings, reversing the nominal size-based weak/strong roles (r14–r16).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Realizable convex-class regression; and bounded finite-sample non-realizable regression
reader_labels.reason: Theorems 1 and 2 state conditional bounds in which the misfit reduces the strong student's true error relative to the weak model's error, up to finite-sample and non-realizability terms (r20–r21).
